Why More Than One Opinion Leads to Better Choices

Last spring my cousin Dana had to decide between two colleges. One was a large state university close to home with a generous scholarship. The other was a small private school three states away with a better program in marine biology, the field she had loved since she was ten. She asked her parents, and they said to take the scholarship. She asked her best friend, who told her to follow the marine biology. Then she asked her old science teacher, who said something neither of them had mentioned: the state university ran a summer research partnership with a coastal lab, so she might get both. Each opinion changed the shape of the decision. Dana's story shows why asking more than one person usually leads to a better choice than asking only one.

The first reason is that every person sees a problem from a different position. Dana's parents were thinking about debt, because they had lived through years of paying off loans. Her friend was thinking about happiness, because she knew how often Dana talked about the ocean. Neither was wrong, but each was looking at only part of the picture. When someone asks only one person, they get one slice of the situation and may mistake it for the whole. When they ask several, the slices begin to overlap, and the person can see which concerns matter most and which are simply one individual's worry.

The second reason is that different people know different facts. Advice is not only a matter of taste. It is often a matter of information. Dana's teacher knew about the coastal lab partnership because he had sent two former students there. Her parents had no idea it existed, and her friend had never looked into it. If Dana had stopped after the first conversation, she would have made her choice without a piece of knowledge that changed everything. The same thing happens when people buy a used car. A friend who loves driving may talk about how smooth it feels, while a mechanic notices rust under the frame. Neither can replace the other, and a buyer who hears both is far less likely to be surprised later.

A third benefit is that multiple opinions protect against bias. Every adviser has some stake, even if it is small. Dana's parents wanted her closer to home, partly because they would miss her. Her friend, who was moving away herself, may have liked the idea of Dana being bold too. These feelings are natural and rarely dishonest, but they tilt advice in a direction. When several people disagree, the tilts tend to cancel each other out, and what remains is more reliable. Doctors understand this, which is why patients facing a serious diagnosis are often encouraged to get a second opinion. A second doctor has no reason to protect the first one's conclusion, and if both agree, the patient can proceed with real confidence.

Finally, hearing several views helps a person understand their own thinking. When Dana listened to her parents, she noticed that she felt defensive, and that told her something. When she listened to her friend, she felt relieved. Those reactions were data about what she wanted. Disagreement forced her to explain her reasons out loud, and in doing so she sorted out her own priorities. A single adviser can easily become a voice that simply gets obeyed or ignored. A group of advisers makes the person do the actual work of weighing.

None of this means that more is always better. If someone asks twenty people, the answers may become a noisy pile that creates paralysis rather than clarity, and it is wise to choose advisers who know the subject or know the person well. In the end, the decision still belongs to the one who has to live with it. But a small, varied set of voices, perhaps three or four, gives a person facts they lacked, perspectives they missed, and a check on anyone's hidden bias.

Dana ended up at the state university and joined the coastal lab the following summer. She says she would have chosen differently, and probably worse, if she had listened only to the first person who answered. Asking around did not make the choice for her. It made the choice informed, and that is what good advice is supposed to do.
